Robin
January 6th..

Five years ago.  I remember the crowds, the singing, the joy.  I remember talking with old Chinese women, (several of them) who had tears in their eyes, begging us native born Americans not to surrender to socialism and communism.  I remember thinking, "I have never seen so many people in one place at one time."  Honestly, it was shoulder-to-shoulder.  I remember singing "God Bless America" near the scaffolding on the western steps of the capitol.  I remember seeing nuns, boys scouts, families, veterans, and a very jovial bunch of South Carolinians drinking, (I think), pirated mint juleps. 

I remember getting pepper-sprayed, even though I did nothing to deserve it.  I didn't resent the capitol police, even with the one fat guy who appeared to enjoy dousing the crowd from a kind of pepper-spray super-soaker.  I can remember one protestor getting milk poured in his eyes and begging to be relieved from the pain.  It was like any boisterous First Amendment protest I've ever attended.  I counted it a good day.  From where I was standing, I couldn't see any of the altercations near the entrances to the capitol.  

When I got back to my hotel, I witnessed the limited incidents of violence CNN played on a continuous loop.  I stuck around in DC for a few days and began to sense I was considered an "insurrectionist" merely for being there.  I thought to myself "no reasonable jury could convict people merely for protesting, right?  They didn't crack down on the BLM protesters who forced the president into the bunker, right?"

Boy, was I naive.  When I returned home, Sarah said she felt threatened.  An anonymous chat window correspondent hoped that all the Smiths would be burned alive in their homes.  When I reported it, the detective was more interested in my activities in DC. One wife of a local law enforcement officer kept wondering if I was "okay."  (I kept thinking to myself, 'does she know something I don't?")  

A friend I met after the event told me an FBI SWAT team pointed red laser target dots at his chest, forced him to sit outside in the cold, while his 12 year old daughter remained inside during the search.  He was sworn at, abused, and ultimately subjected to three years of prosecution and prison.  He never went inside the building.  He gave first aid to people who were wounded by the capitol police.  He was pardoned by President Trump, like all the others, because it really was a modern day witch hunt.

An inside source told me that in Southern California, all of the FBI people who participated in the persecution of the J6 political prisoners have been "walked out of the building." I don't know if that's true, but I can hope.  Political law enforcement means the end of the republic.

Praise God it's over.  Even if you hate everything about the J6 protestors, you really should ask yourself, "do I want to live in a country where justice changes with every election."
